title: Hillel on the roof (Yoma 35b)
hookLine: too poor for the fee, young Hillel lay on the skylight in the snow to hear the lesson

lines: A POOR YOUNG MAN IN JERUSALEM.
cards: Think of the last time you really wanted to be somewhere and couldn't afford it. A concert. A class.
A trip your friends were taking. You stood outside it, in a way. Before Hillel was the great Hillel, he was a poor young man from Babylonia, working for tiny wages in Jerusalem.
The best teachers in the city taught in a study house with a guard at the door and a fee to get in. One winter day he didn't have the fee. So what did he do?

teach.h: HALF FOR THE GUARD, HALF FOR HOME.
teach.b: The story is in the Talmud, tractate Yoma. Every day Hillel worked and earned a small coin. Half went to the guard of the study house, where the teachers Shemaya and Avtalyon taught.
Half fed his family. One day he earned nothing, and the guard wouldn't let him in.

teach.h: ONTO THE ROOF, BY THE SKYLIGHT.
teach.b: So Hillel climbed onto the roof and lay down by the skylight, to hear the words of the living God from their mouths. It was a Friday in the dead of winter, and snow began to fall. He stayed.
In the morning, Shemaya said to Avtalyon: my brother, every day this house is bright, and today it's dark. Is it cloudy? They looked up and saw the shape of a man in the skylight.

They climbed up and found Hillel under a thick layer of snow. They brought him down, washed him, rubbed him with oil, and sat him by the fire, though it was Shabbat. This one, they said, is worth breaking the Sabbath for.
Saving a life overrides Shabbat for anyone; the line is their way of saying how much they loved him. The Talmud tells the story for a reason.
When poor people are asked why they didn't learn, it says, the answer comes back: were you poorer than Hillel? That's a hard question. But it isn't a scolding.
Learning finds a way in, even through the roof.

how: Jewish tradition treats Torah study as open to everyone, rich or poor, and the story of Hillel on the roof is often told to children and adults to show how much learning is worth.

a teacher Hillel lay on a snowy roof to hear
the guard who kept poor students out the door

p: lay on the skylight in the snow

s: Hillel was born rich and powerful
he was a poor young man from Babylonia, working for tiny wages.
his teachers noticed him because the room was dark
the snow on the skylight blocked the light.
the story happened on a summer evening

games.q: you're young Hillel. you earned nothing today and the guard won't let you in. what do you do?
o: go home and come back tomorrow.
climb onto the roof and listen at the skylight.
games.why: he climbed up and lay by the skylight to hear the lesson, and stayed even when the snow buried him.

practice: Think of something you want to learn and keep putting off, a language, an instrument, a text, how to fix the thing that keeps breaking, and name the guard at its door: time, money, feeling too old, feeling behind.
Now picture the skylight, one small way in anyway: a free library book, ten minutes before bed, a question to someone who knows. Hold that one way in.

wordCard.voice: Shemaya, one of the two teachers Hillel lay on a snowy skylight to hear. Too poor to pay the guard, Hillel listened from the roof, and Shemaya and his partner Avtalyon said he was worth breaking Shabbat for.

orig.note: Hebrew: Shemaya and Avtalyon, the teachers Hillel climbed the roof to hear.

carryVoice: Your line: listen through the snow. Hillel found his way in from the roof. Two hundred seventy-four, done.
